object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer in the system. Every account has an account number, which everything hangs off. If an account closes and the same company returns, they get a new number and are treated as a new customer.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Unique six-digit sequential identifier of an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product. Identified by a subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product sold by the company, identified by a product code. Currently three: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: Identifying code of a product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that generates the invoice line -- what the customer pays and how often. Identified by a plan code. Not the same as a feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Identifying code of a price plan, e.g. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: What the customer gets -- the feature bundle (seats, API access, SSO). Identified by name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise). No code exists.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: Unique name identifying a feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. ... A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.
Never neither. Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.
Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused; overlaps confusingly with status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with a change ID, effective date, requester, and the new price plan. Objectifies the subscription-plan-change relationship.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier of a plan change record.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: and it takes effect, and those are different dates... records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; derived from the price plan price normalised to a month and the billing period, not stored.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue.
It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.

ambiguities.description: Two (or three) different concepts are all called 'plan': the price plan (billing artefact), the feature bundle (what the customer gets), and a sales-negotiated deal that 'frequently matches neither'. The transcript explicitly leaves the sales-team usage unresolved and out of scope. Should the sales 'plan' concept be modeled at all, and if so how does it relate to PricePlan/FeatureBundle?

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.
Only that we still call three different things "plan" and this document won't fix that.

ambiguities.description: The PausedFlag overlaps confusingly with SubscriptionStatus -- a subscription can be 'active' and 'paused' simultaneously, and querying for active subscriptions incorrectly returns paused ones. It's unclear whether Paused should be modeled as an exclusion constraint against certain statuses, or left as an independent, unconstrained boolean as the business currently (problematically) has it.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: Whether mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions should result in a refund, credit, or run-to-term is explicitly parked as undecided business policy. The current system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund) is captured, but ad hoc manual credits outside the subscription model exist and are not represented. Should a future 'refund/credit' concept be modeled once policy is decided?

source_references.excerpt: Is there a rule today that I could write down? ... What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term ... is undecided.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between Subscription and its 'current' PricePlan is asserted to be a denormalised, maintained-by-process field, while the true history is in PlanChange records. It's stated that if the two disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is treated as a bug -- but no explicit subset/equality constraint mechanism was described for keeping them in sync. Should a formal constraint (e.g., current plan on Subscription must equal the price plan of the most recent PlanChange by effective date) be added?

source_references.excerpt: Since the reporting rebuild. It's maintained by the change process, nobody sets it by hand. ... if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: A fourth product is 'in discovery' but not yet defined -- the ProductCode value constraint of exactly {CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT} may need revision soon. Should the value constraint be treated as closed/fixed or open-ended given a fourth product is anticipated?

source_references.excerpt: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: Account identification: company name is explicitly not unique (four accounts named 'Acme'), and email belongs to the Contact, not the Account -- but no Contact entity or its relationship to Account was elaborated in this session. Is a Contact entity out of scope for this model, or should it be captured with its own identifier/relationship to Account?

source_references.excerpt: Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called "Acme." Email is on the contact, not the account.
